content.rationale:
The commitment: every draft record is the one JSON document its handle names — `<root>/<handle>.json` under the work-state registry `.deccy/work/` — the stored records are found only by scanning that directory, and a record is read only through the form `schemas/work.json` fixes together with the agreement between the document's `handle` field and the filename that gives it. `src/draft_registry.rs` is that commitment as Rust. `path_for` derives the path a handle names; `write` creates the registry root when it is not there and stores one document at that path, replacing the document already there rather than appending; `read` returns a document only when it conforms to the carried schema and carries its own handle; `scan` returns every document in the directory keyed by the handle its filename gives, and no records when the directory is not there; `remove` deletes exactly the document at `path_for(root, handle)` and nothing else; and every refusal is an `Error` value naming the path it refused — never a panic, never a document surfaced as a record, never one passed over silently.

The path is the handle and nothing else (`rqtowtqn`). `path_for` composes `<root>/<handle>.json` and stops there: no per-draft subdirectory, no sharded directory, no index file, no second layout, and no lookup that must be asked before the path is known. `write` stores the record at exactly that path — one file per handle — and `read` opens exactly that path, so a holder of a handle names the document without asking anything else (`owyntkvw`). Because the path is the handle, the filename is the handle: `write` takes the document's own `handle` field as the name of the file it writes, and a document that carries no handle string names no file at all, so it is refused with `Invalid` against the registry root rather than guessed at from some other field. A second write under one handle writes the same path again, and `fs::write` replaces the file there, so a rewrite leaves one document holding the record and never two; that is the storage side of "exactly one JSON document at `<handle>.json`" (`rqtowtqn`, `twpvqstu`).

The document is the whole record, so the directory is the whole registry (`twpvqstu`). Nothing of a record is kept outside its document — no side file per handle, no summary list, no index beside the documents — and this module therefore has no second place to write and no second place to read. Discovery is `scan`, which reads the directory and returns the documents it finds; an index would be a copy of that list which the documents could contradict and which every write would have to maintain, so there is none. The module deletes nothing at landing: a landed record is kept, so the directory's contents do not shrink when a draft lands and a scan is complete without consulting any record's state or trusting that a deletion happened. Removal is the store's one explicit deletion and it is a path operation: `remove` deletes exactly the document at `<root>/<handle>.json` — the record the caller names as discarded — and leaves every other document byte-identical, whether it is landed or open, whether this module wrote it or it was placed there by hand. It scans nothing, reads nothing and checks no other record's form, so a document a `read` would refuse beside the target neither blocks the removal nor is repaired by it; the target itself is removed without being interpreted, because a discarded record's form is not what the removal is asked about. Because a record placed in the directory by any means is a record — the store never had a private registration step — `scan` does not consult a list of what was written through `write`; it reads the files that are there.

The registry is a directory of untracked state (`nolspvpw`), and this module is written for that and nothing else. It works on filesystem paths under the root it is handed: it holds no repository, no change id, no node set and no working copy, and it never asks where the root came from or whether the directory is tracked. The root arrives as a parameter of every entry point for that reason — the caller names the registry directory, so the module depends on no current directory and no environment, and a test can hand it a temporary directory without a repository behind it. The module touches nothing outside that root: every path it reads, writes or lists is `<root>` or a document directly under it, and the only directory it creates is the root itself — with a missing ancestor of it when the root is nested under one, since a directory cannot otherwise be made — on the first write.

The first `write` creates the root when it is not there: `.deccy/work/` is the untracked-state directory the registry lives in (`nolspvpw`), a fresh repository has no reason to hold an empty one, and the record being stored is what makes it a registry — so the first `deccy draft` succeeds instead of failing on a directory nobody had yet created. Creation is the write's, not a caller's errand: no entry point asks for a root that must already exist, `path_for` stays a pure path composition, `read` still answers `Missing` and `scan` still answers an empty list for a root that is not there, and only the operation that stores a document brings the directory into being — creating a missing ancestor along with it when the root is nested, and placing no file anywhere except the record's own path under the root. The schema check runs before the root is created and before anything is stored, so a document the check refuses stores nothing and, in particular, leaves no registry behind; a later write finds the root already there and `create_dir_all` changes nothing.

The handle is the identity, and the other fields are references (`owyntkvw`). Every key in this module is a handle: `path_for` takes one, `write` takes the document's own, `read` takes one, and `scan` keys each returned pair by the handle its filename gives. The record's node, its edit and its workspace are references and are never used as keys here — no lookup addresses a record by node or by edit, and no index groups records by either, because one node may be named by several records at once and one edit by the records of every node it touches; a key that names many records is not a key. The module does not read the `node` or `edit` fields at all, and it does not check that a node id resolves, which is a graph rule and not a storage rule.

The document's form is `schemas/work.json`, carried in the binary (`wrvsxwmq`). The file is embedded with `include_str!` — the compiled binary never reads a schema out of the repository at run time — and it is compiled once per process by the `jsonschema` crate (`zmmyomyp`) over a value decoded by serde_json (`orrvsxqq`). The check is the validator's, not a hand-written walk over the fields: no required field, enum, closed object or nested workspace is restated in Rust, so the schema stays the one copy of the record's form and a change to the artifact changes every reader at once. Because the schema is the record's whole form and closed at both levels, the same check runs before `write` stores a document — and before it creates the root the document lands in — so what the directory holds is then the form every reader checks, not merely the form some writer meant (the premise `wrvsxwmq` states for every writer and reader of the registry). A document that fails the check is refused with `Invalid`, naming the path it would have been stored at, and nothing is written.

The read applies the two grounds the read rule fixes (`ntypuupx`). A path with no document is absence, not a record (`rqtowtqn`). A document that is not JSON is `NotJson`, carrying the parser's reason. A document that parses but does not conform to `schemas/work.json` is `Invalid`, carrying the validator's reasons. A document that conforms but whose `handle` field is a different string from the handle its filename gives is `HandleMismatch`, carrying the path, the filename's handle and the document's — the schema types the handle as any non-empty string, so shape alone cannot refuse this document, and the filename-is-the-handle rule is what does. The order matters: the schema check runs first, so a malformed document is refused for its form, and the handle comparison runs on documents that are already records by shape, so a mismatch is never reported for a field the schema already rejected. Every ground returns `Err` — no `Option`, no panic, no fallback — and every variant carries the path, which `Display` names, so a refusal made anywhere in the CLI is a refusal that names the record it refused.

`scan` routes every document through the same read, so the refusal rule holds for discovery too (`ntypuupx`). A document that a read refuses makes the scan refuse rather than vanish from the listing: a record that is present and malformed must not become indistinguishable from a record that is absent, which is exactly what skipping it silently would do. Names that are not `.json` documents are not records and are not returned; a `.json` name that is not UTF-8 names no handle a JSON document could carry, so it is refused rather than dropped. What `scan` returns is every record that is there, keyed by handle, so the listing is the registry and not a view of it.

Absence has a meaning of its own (`rqtowtqn`). `read` of a handle the directory does not name is `Missing` with that path — a record that is not there, not an empty record and not a failure of form — `scan` of a directory that is not there is an empty list, because a registry that does not exist holds no records, and `remove` of a handle the directory does not name is `Missing` with that path and deletes nothing, because the record being discarded is not there; the registry is the documents that are there. The remaining variant is `Io`: a path that cannot be read, listed or written, whose message names the path it happened at, since no rule about the record's form explains a filesystem failure. That is the whole refusal surface — absence, not-JSON, invalid form, handle disagreement, io — and each variant answers a rule already stated above rather than adding one.

The module is the single flat file `src/draft_registry.rs` (`szmuyqrq`): no nested module directory, no `mod.rs`, no companion file, and no helper crate. It uses nothing of the crate it is compiled in — no `crate::` item, no type or constant borrowed from a neighbour — because a self-contained test crate includes it alone (`knqkxzns`) and because everything it needs is the standard library plus the two crates the prerequisites fix: serde_json for the document (`orrvsxqq`) and jsonschema for the check (`zmmyomyp`). None of the four entry points assumes anything about the rest of the binary, so the same file is the module whichever crate declares it.

Deliberately outside, because each is a separate commitment: how a handle is minted, what its alphabet or length is, and whether it is generated from anything (`owyntkvw` mints it) — this module accepts any handle string and checks nothing about its shape; the state lifecycle, the retention rule beyond "a landed record is still a record a scan returns", and what a caller does after a removal beyond the store deleting the one named document; the field set, the enum and the closed objects, which are the schema's (`wrvsxwmq`) and are never restated here; the encoding of the content-identity base; the permissions and ownership of the root the first write creates, and whether anything else in `.deccy/work/` sits beside the records; atomicity, flushing, durability and what a write that fails after the check leaves behind; concurrent writers and locking; the rendering and exit status of a listing verb, and whether a record and the workspace it names can drift. A store can name, write, read, scan and remove with none of these settled, and settling any of them would not change what this module does. The scan's ordering by handle is a repeatability choice of the implementation, not a commitment: no consumer may depend on the order.

No clause carries a verdict or evidence: the node states what the store does with a document, and which document failed a check is a finding of a run, not content of this decision.
